summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Once an agency with temporary custody moves for permanent custody, a juvenile court has no authority to order a planned permanent living arrangement that the agency has not requested, because that disposition leaves the child in limbo and delays a permanent home.
key_cases.relevance: It limits the dispositions a court may impose over the agency's objection once a child is in foster care under temporary custody.
key_cases.quote: Children who age out of foster care lack the emotional support system and the financial stability of a permanent custody or adoptive relationship.

key_cases.holding: Except for narrowly defined statutory exceptions the state must have made reasonable efforts to reunify the family before parental rights are terminated, but the specific R.C. 2151.419(A)(1) reasonable-efforts determination applies only at the enumerated removal and disposition hearings and not at a hearing on an R.C. 2151.413 permanent-custody motion, where the agency must prove reasonable efforts only if it has not already done so.
key_cases.relevance: Removal to foster care must be preceded and accompanied by proven efforts to prevent or end the out-of-home placement.
key_cases.quote: we hold that, except for a few narrowly defined exceptions, the state must have made reasonable efforts to reunify the family prior to the termination of parental rights

key_cases.holding: The agency need not prove that no suitable relative was available before permanent custody may be granted; the availability of a placement that would avoid termination is one relevant factor in the R.C. 2151.414(D) weighing, not a controlling one.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that a foster placement may become the permanent plan without the agency having to disprove every less restrictive alternative.
key_cases.quote: The statute does not make the availability of a placement that would not require a termination of parental rights an all-controlling factor.

key_cases.holding: An adjudication of abuse, dependency or neglect coupled with an award of temporary custody under R.C. 2151.353(A)(2) is a final order that must be appealed within 30 days under App.R. 4(A), and App.R. 4(B)(5) gives no second opportunity to appeal that adjudication after the final dispositional order terminating parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: A parent contesting the placement of a child in agency temporary custody must appeal the adjudication-and-temporary-custody entry itself rather than wait for a later disposition.
key_cases.quote: App.R. 4(B)(5) does not apply to adjudication orders that include a finding of neglect, abuse, or dependency and a grant of temporary custody to a children services agency

key_cases.holding: After a child has been adjudicated dependent, a juvenile court need not make a separate finding of parental unfitness before awarding permanent custody under R.C. 2151.353(D); such an award is justified only when it is in the child's best interests, because a parent's fitness is one factor and parental interests are subordinated to the child's welfare.
key_cases.relevance: The Court treats permanent commitment as the most serious dispositional alternative and reads R.C. 2151.01(C) to permit separating a child from parents only when necessary for the child's welfare or public safety.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that an award of permanent custody, pursuant to R. C. 2151.353(D), is only justified when it is in the "best interests" of the child

key_cases.case_name: Pittman v. Cuyahoga Cty. Dept. of Children & Family Servs.
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of immunity to an Ohio caseworker, holding her absolutely immune for the juvenile complaint and the affidavits she filed in her advocacy capacity, and qualifiedly immune on the father's substantive and procedural due process claims because Ohio law places responsibility for placement decisions and for notice of custody proceedings on the juvenile court rather than on the caseworker.
key_cases.relevance: Placement decisions belong to the juvenile court, and Ohio law gives a parent the means to contest placement at the dispositional hearing and to propose a change to the case plan at any time.
key_cases.quote: it is the juvenile court's responsibility to ensure that Pittman received adequate notice of the custody proceedings

timeline_requirements.deadline: Filed with the court before the adjudicatory hearing, no later than 30 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Earlier of the date the complaint was filed or the child was first placed in shelter care
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not stated in the statute; all parts of the case plan must be completed by the earlier of 30 days after the adjudicatory hearing or the date of the dispositional hearing
